newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: Little growth seen in Dutch-German trade.
newsitem.headline: Little growth seen in Dutch-German trade.

text.p: Dutch-German trade will probably slow down further in 1997 and subsequent years, Karl-Heinz Roesener, president of the Dutch-German chamber of commerce told a news conference on Tuesday.
"We have to acknowledge that economic development is no longer centred in central Europe but rather in other regions, such as South-East Asia," Roesener said.
Although western industrial countries will remain the most important markets for both Germany and the Netherlands, outlets outside Europe will gain significance, he said.
Consequently trade with countries in other regions was likely to grow faster than intra-European and Dutch-German trade flows, Roesener added.
The total value of Dutch-German trade slipped by 0.4 percent to 115 billion marks in 1996.
Dutch exports to Germany fell one percent to 57.5 billion marks, equivalent to 28 percent of all German imports.
Excluding energy products -- which rose nearly 25 percent to 11.1 billion marks -- Dutch exports to Germany fell 5.9 percent.
Dutch exports of manufactured and semi-manufactured goods fell 1.3 percent to 38.3 billion marks, while exports of food and agricultural products fell 3.2 percent to 14.2 billion.
German exports to the Netherlands were broadly steady at 57.3 billion, accounting for 21 percent of all Dutch imports.
German exports of food and agricultural products to the Netherlands rose 3.7 percent to 6.24 billion marks in 1996.
Exports of German manufactured and semi-manufactured goods to the Netherlands fell 1.1 percent to 48.1 billion marks.
Germany remained the Netherland's biggest trading partner in 1996. France was Germany's biggest trading partner, but the Netherlands overtook Italy to claim second place.
Roesener said the Netherlands had attracted 38 percent of Germany's total foreign direct investment of four billion marks in 1996, more than any other country.
Dutch foreign direct investment totalled $1 billion in 1996, of which 16 percent went to Germany, he said.

The chamber's vice-president, Gerrit Jan Doeksen, said a delay in the launch of the single European currency would not have a significant impact on Dutch-German trade flows because the guilder and the mark were already closely linked.
"Such a delay would have a negative impact on Europe as a whole. Within that picture, Dutch-German relationships would be more or less stable, but at a lower level," Doeksen said.
